title: Why the Muslim World Fell Behind
author: Ahmet Kuru
content:
![Why the Muslim World Fell
Behind](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/10/AP20136582782443.jpg)

Why is the Islamic world socioeconomically underdeveloped? When we compare
Muslim-majority countries not only with Western countries but also with the
rest of the world in terms of Gross National Income per capita, they rank
below average, despite their substantial oil revenues. The same is true when
it comes to life expectancy, years of schooling, and literacy rate. What is
more, of fifty Muslim-majority countries, none is a liberal democracy, and
only a few of them are categorized as electoral democracies, compared to
roughly half of all other countries worldwide.

But to raise the question of why this is the case in educated circles in the
West is almost taboo, as I discovered this when I was working on [_a
book_](https://urldefense.com/v3/__https:/www.cambridge.org/core/books/islam-
authoritarianism-and-
underdevelopment/E337124CD3A3DDAB72136E0B9FC898EB__;!!H7yp__TR!amC1zPSmqdtENVfEK_ZxKVK6GkrtL7joUaYQ-
FX_pfP3QWzSePPtchyvJ0Tzc9ANZWukPuiooMw78thF0r0ls6FD$?ref=compactmag.com) on
the topic. At the time, a colleague in my department suggested I get it
published in Turkish and Arabic, but not English; he was concerned that the
book would fuel Islamophobia. The book, _Islam, Authoritarianism, and
Underdevelopment_ , appeared in 2019 in English and has since been translated
into fifteen languages; it has been received differently in the West and in
Muslim-majority countries. While Western scholars have accused me of
Orientalism and Eurocentrism, editions published in Turkey, Bosnia, Lebanon,
Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Indonesia have been well received as an overdue
analysis of the problems in these societies.

Do I blame Islam for underdevelopment? No. Religious ideas matter, but they
exist within a broader political, social, and material context. As is well-
known, Islam was compatible with remarkable scientific and economic progress
in its early history. For the majority of Western scholars, Western
colonialism is what brought this earlier progress to an end and keeps these
societies behind. I disagree. Although colonialism and imperialism have been
detrimental, they are not unique to the Muslim world. From Latin America to
East Asia, many countries faced similar conditions, but they have found ways
to develop and democratize anyway. Furthermore, the Muslim world started to
lag behind Western Europe before widespread colonization began.

> "Islam was compatible with remarkable scientific and economic progress in
> its early history."

For many Western scholars, to place too much emphasis on Muslim societies'
historical stagnation is to judge them by European standards through an
Orientalist lens. It is time to question this approach. Although Edward Said's
_Orientalism_ was a paradigm-shifting book a half-century ago, its central
concept is now used lazily to dismiss scholarship with inconvenient
conclusions. In any case, there is an obvious way to avoid the Orientalist
charge: to judge the contemporary Muslim world by its own historical
achievements. In an earlier era, Muslim societies gave the world philosophers,
scientists, and mathematicians whose influence persists to this day, while
also playing a pivotal role in intercontinental trade, all at a time when
Europe was intellectually and economically marginal. During that period,
Muslims taught Europeans the Hindu-Arabic numeral system, optics, and
Aristotelian philosophy, among other novelties.

In the eleventh and twelfth centuries, however, the Muslim world and Western
Europe began to reverse roles. The relations between religious, political,
intellectual, and economic classes played a central position in this process.
In early Islamic history, Islamic scholars (the _ulema_) generally regarded
close entanglements with political authorities as corrupting; they preferred
to be funded by commerce and maintained close relations with merchants. At
that time, most Islamic scholars and their families worked in commerce; a
small minority received public money. The resulting independence from
political power was a boon to intellectual and economic development.

However, the Muslim world underwent a transformation in the eleventh and
twelfth centuries. Sectarianism was at the center of it. The Abbasid caliphs
in Baghdad, severely weakened by the rising Shii powers throughout the Middle
East and North Africa, called for the unification of Sunnis to meet this
threat. The caliphs declared a "Sunni creed," and those whose views were
deemed to contradict this creed, including certain Shiis, rationalist
theologians, and philosophers, were declared to be apostates and faced the
threat of execution.

This transformation led to a partnership between religious and political
authorities. This alliance gradually marginalized the philosophers and
merchants, leading to long-lasting scientific and economic stagnation in the
Muslim world. There were later attempts to reform religio-political
institutions in the Muslim world, but the ulema and their monarchical partners
used apostasy laws, state power, and the monopoly on education through
madrasas to preserve the status quo. Between the fifteenth and nineteenth
centuries, Muslims established three empires: the Sunni Ottoman, the Shii
Safavid, and the Sunni-run (but non-sectarian) Mughal empires, which ruled a
vast geography from the Balkans to Bengal. These empires were militarily
powerful, but they failed to revive early Muslims' intellectual and economic
dynamism because their ulema-state alliances virtually eliminated philosophers
and marginalized merchants.

While the Muslim world was losing its intellectual and economic momentum,
Western Europe experienced the opposite trajectory after the eleventh and
twelfth centuries, with the distinction between church and state, opening of
universities, and the rise of a powerful merchant class.

In their early history, Muslim societies were so dynamic that when they saw an
innovation, such as Chinese papermaking, they immediately employed it. Western
European societies opened the first paper factory centuries after Muslims did.
But as class relations changed, so did attitudes toward innovation. Muslims
waited for centuries to adopt new technologies and tools developed in Western
Europe, such as the printing press, telescope, and medical research on
cadavers.

By the nineteenth century, there was almost a consensus among the Muslim
elite, especially in Istanbul and Cairo, that Muslim societies needed to
reform to catch up with the West. These political elites were not
"Orientalists"; they simply knew the conditions of their own countries in
comparison to the West. As the Ottoman bureaucrat and intellectual Ziya Pasha,
who lived between 1829 and 1880, wrote in a famous poem: "I traveled through
the lands of infidels and saw cities and mansions,/ I wandered through the
realm of Islam and saw total ruins."

Yet the reform attempts in the nineteenth and the twentieth centuries were
only partially successful. The legacy of centuries of intellectual and
economic stagnation proved difficult for Muslim societies to overcome.
Although reformist bureaucrats often sidelined the ulema, they never truly
tried to revive intellectual and bourgeois classes. Most of the reformers had
military backgrounds, and they were too statist to appreciate free speech and
the free market. Over the past half-century, the _ulema_ -state alliance has
reasserted its power across much of the Muslim world in different forms:
through the Wahhabi-Saudi alliance in the Arabian Peninsula, the Islamic
Revolution in Iran, the sharia courts-military nexus in Pakistan, the Azhar-
military alliance in Egypt, and the Diyanet-elected politicians alliance in
Turkey.

What is to be done? The first task is to be honest about the situation and
refuse to cover up problems with charges of Orientalism or laments over the
colonial legacy. Although Western colonialism and imperialism damaged many
Muslim countries and exploited their resources, a narrow focus on this history
has distracted Muslims from addressing their internal problems and reforming
their institutions. An honest retelling of the region's history does not
contribute to Islamophobia. For example, it has been frequently claimed that
Islam, unlike Christianity, rejects the separation of church and state, and is
therefore incompatible with liberal democracy. But an analysis of Islamic
history reveals that there was a certain level of religion-state separation in
early Islamic history, which contributed to Islam's scientific and economic
golden age. The _ulema_ -state alliance is neither a theological necessity of
Islam nor a continuous historical fact.

This historical interpretation suggests that contemporary Muslims can redesign
the relationship between their religion and their states in a way that would
promote intellectual and economic creativity, as well as allowing for
liberalization and democratization. Muslims do not need to be Westernized for
such a reform to take place; their early history provides an authentic
inspiration.
